hooks.text: Walk into any store and look at the price tags. Nine ninety-nine. Nineteen ninety-nine. Four ninety-nine. Almost nothing costs exactly ten dollars.

chapters.title: The Puzzle
chapters.text: Walk into any store and look at the price tags. Nine ninety-nine. Nineteen ninety-nine. Four ninety-nine. Almost nothing costs exactly ten dollars. One cent less. That is all it is. Nobody gets rich or poor from a single penny. So why does nearly every store do it? The answer is a mix of an old story about thieves, a strange quirk in how your brain reads numbers, and one very expensive mistake by a famous American store.

chapters.title: The Cash Register Story
chapters.text: The most famous explanation goes back to the late eighteen hundreds, and the cash register. If something cost exactly one dollar, a dishonest clerk could take your dollar, skip the register, and quietly keep it. But at ninety-nine cents, they had to open the drawer to give you change. And opening the drawer rang a bell, and left a record. It is a great story. But there is little hard evidence that stores really chose odd prices for that reason. Today, it is best treated as a legend. And even if it was true once, it does not explain why online stores, with no cashiers at all, still charge nine ninety-nine. For that, we need to look inside your head.

chapters.title: The Left-Digit Trick
chapters.text: We read numbers from left to right. And the first digit hits the hardest. In two thousand five, marketing researchers Manoj Thomas and Vicki Morwitz ran five experiments on this. They found that a price like two ninety-nine can feel noticeably smaller than three dollars, even though the gap is one cent. But the trick mostly works when the first digit changes. Three dollars to two ninety-nine feels like a real drop. Three sixty to three fifty-nine barely registers. Your brain does not do the subtraction. It grabs the first digit, takes a shortcut, and moves on. Stores simply design their prices around that shortcut.

chapters.title: The Catalog Experiment
chapters.text: But does it actually change what people buy? In two thousand three, Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester tested it with a real women's clothing catalog. They printed different versions of the catalog. The same dress appeared at forty-four, forty-nine, or fifty-four dollars, depending on which copy you received. The result surprised a lot of people. The forty-nine dollar version sold the most. More than the cheaper price of forty-four. Across their three experiments, a nine at the end raised demand every time. And the effect was strongest on new items, where shoppers had no idea what a fair price was.

chapters.title: The Store That Said No
chapters.text: So what happens if a store decides to stop playing the game? In twenty twelve, the American chain J.C. Penney found out. Its new boss, Ron Johnson, launched a plan called Fair and Square. Hundreds of sales events a year were cut to about a dozen, and a price like nineteen ninety-nine became a clean twenty dollars. It sounded honest. Customers hated it. That year, sales fell by about a quarter, and the company lost nearly a billion dollars. Within about a year and a half, Johnson was gone, and the sales and the old-style pricing came back.

chapters.title: The Lesson
chapters.text: But round numbers are not always the enemy. In twenty fifteen, researchers Monica Wadhwa and Kuangjie Zhang found that round prices can feel right when we buy with our hearts, like a holiday or a gift, while precise prices suit practical purchases. That is why a luxury handbag often says two thousand dollars, while a bottle of shampoo says four ninety-nine. So a price is never just a number. It is a message, written for the shortcuts in your brain. And now you know how to read it. If you enjoyed this, subscribe so you don't miss the next puzzle. And tell us in the comments: what is the strangest price you have ever seen?
